snippet.title: They Sold Mortgages They Knew Were Bad
snippet.description:
On November 19, 2013, the Justice Department announced a record $13 billion settlement with JPMorgan Chase — then the largest settlement with a single entity in American history — resolving federal and state civil claims over residential mortgage-backed securities (RMBS) packaged, marketed, and sold by JPMorgan, Bear Stearns, and Washington Mutual before January 1, 2009. Of the total, $9 billion was cash: a $2 billion civil penalty, $1.4 billion to the National Credit Union Administration, $4 billion to the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and the rest to states and the FDIC. The remaining $4 billion was consumer relief — mortgage modifications, principal reductions, and anti-blight spending. In an accompanying statement of facts, JPMorgan acknowledged it had regularly told RMBS investors that the underlying loans complied with underwriting guidelines while its own employees knew they did not. The deal did not resolve any criminal exposure for the bank or its employees, nor any claims against individuals. CEO Jamie Dimon had negotiated directly with Attorney General Eric Holder, and the talks had nearly collapsed weeks earlier. The settlement opened the floodgates: Citigroup paid $7 billion in July 2014, Bank of America $16.65 billion that August — the new record — followed by Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and others. What was never solved was the accountability question: no senior executive at any major bank faced criminal charges over the mortgage crisis, and the settlements resolved civil claims only.

snippet.title: Your AI Assistant Got Hacked — Your Bank Says: Not Our Problem #AI
snippet.description:
Picture this. You hand your AI assistant your bank login. It pays your bills, watches your spending, and moves your money while you sleep. One morning, you wake up, and your account is empty. You call the bank. And the bank says, sorry, you authorized it. That is not a hypothetical anymore. This week, Citibank, one of the biggest banks in America, quietly rewrote its customer agreement. If you give your bank login to an AI agent, and that agent gets hacked, the money a criminal takes is your problem, not the bank's.

Citi added a brand new section, Section H, to its Online User Agreement. If you give your login credentials to an AI agent, Citi will treat anything that agent does as something you authorized — even if those credentials later get shared, leaked, or stolen. The bank says it has no obligation to investigate. You are responsible for the agent's mistakes, and for watching what it does. A separate agreement on online funds transfers goes further: any transfer an AI agent starts counts as authorized by you, even if it conflicts with what you actually told the agent. Citi can cut off any third-party AI agent's access at any time, without warning. One carve-out: AI tools Citi builds itself are excluded.

Citi is not alone. PNC changed its terms the same day, November 18th. Citizens Bank emailed customers this week. JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America moved last month. On November 24th, Wells Fargo's new terms take effect. In about a month, five of the country's largest banks have told customers, in writing, that letting an AI agent into your account comes with a catch: you own whatever happens next.

The trap turns on one word: authorized. Under federal Regulation E, your loss on an unauthorized transfer is normally capped at $50 if you report it within two business days. But by defining everything your AI agent does as authorized by you, in advance, the banks take those transactions out of the unauthorized category before a dispute even starts. No regulator has weighed in on whether that reading holds up. No court has tested it. And the risk is real: in July, test agents escaped a sandbox and attacked Hugging Face; in October, a stolen Fireworks key was used to plant a trojanized Claude Code extension; this week, hackers used the AI-powered attack tool ARTEX against the European Commission. Your agent does not need to be evil to drain your account. It just needs to be fooled.

snippet.title: One Thing Keeps People With Good Salaries Broke
snippet.description:
You earn a good salary but still feel broke by the end of the month, and the usual answer is that you spend too much. This video shows a different cause. We sit down at a leasing desk with three papers: an offer letter for $114,000, an approved application for a bigger apartment, and a bank statement. Along the way you see why so many people are living paycheck to paycheck on a high income, where your paycheck goes before it reaches you, and how little of a $14,000 raise ever shows up in take-home pay. One lease leaves $16 of that raise each month. The other leaves $691. You will also get one number to work out from your own deposits, and a way to tune ordinary bills without cutting the life you already have.

William is an animated narrator; this video was researched and written by the channel’s creator. Educational, not personal advice. snippet.title: 4 aur 7 minute ke hourglass se exact 9 minute? | Hourglass Puzzle (Bank of America, Yahoo)
snippet.description:
Do hourglass hain: ek 4 minute ka, ek 7 minute ka. Exact 9 minute kaise naapoge? Beech mein andaaza nahi chalega: sirf start karo aur palto. Pehli soch: 4 + 4 = 8, 7 + 4 = 11, toh 9 banta hi nahi. Galat! Trick: dono saath mein palto. 4:00 pe 4 wala khatam: palto (7 wale mein 3 bache). 7:00 pe 7 wala khatam: palto (4 wale mein 1 bacha). 8:00 pe 4 wala phir khatam: ab 7 wale ke neeche sirf 1 minute ki ret hai. Palto! Woh 1 minute girta hai aur 9:00 pe khatam: exact 9 minute! Kyun? 4 + 4 = 8, aur 7 wale ka woh 1 minute palat ke: 8 + 1 = 9. snippet.title: Citi y PNC: si autorizas a un agente de IA, respondes tú
snippet.description:
Citi actualizó su acuerdo de usuario en línea: quien le da acceso a su cuenta a un agente de IA de terceros responde por lo que haga ese agente. Según TechCrunch, eso incluye lo que hagan atacantes si la herramienta filtra las credenciales o la hackean. PNC cambió sus términos el 18 de noviembre, Citizens avisó a sus clientes por correo, y JPMorgan y Bank of America anunciaron políticas parecidas en octubre. El contrato de PNC prohíbe dar contraseñas o códigos a un agente y, en general, no permite que inicie pagos sin autorización del banco. Son bancos de EE. UU. y sus términos están sujetos a la ley aplicable. Aun así, la pregunta de quién paga cuando un agente se equivoca llegará a cualquier negocio que automatice pagos. Antes de darle acceso a un agente de IA, lee el contrato, define límites y revisa los movimientos.

snippet.title: The Collapse of Lehman Brothers: $613 Billion and Nobody Charged
snippet.description:
Lehman Brothers collapse explained: how a 158-year-old bank with $639 billion in assets filed the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history on September 15, 2008 — and nobody was ever charged.

At 1:45 a.m. on Monday, September 15, 2008, Lehman Brothers filed for Chapter 11 with $613 billion in debt. This documentary follows the full arc: the cotton store founded in Alabama in 1850, Dick Fuld's 31-to-1 leverage bet on American property, the Repo 105 maneuver that moved $50 billion off the books at quarter-ends, the rescue weekend at the New York Fed where Bank of America walked away and London's regulator blocked Barclays, and the week the failure set fire to the global financial system — the Dow down 504 points, a $62 billion money fund breaking the buck, AIG rescued with $85 billion the next day. It closes with the examiner's 2,200-page autopsy and the question the record still asks: how did the largest bankruptcy in American history produce no criminal charges against anyone?

snippet.title: Chase Said It Wasn't a Hack. Then This Happened.
snippet.description:
On Monday, Chase said its outage was a software bug, "not cyber-related". On Thursday, JPMorgan Chase said its vendors were "the target of a cyber attack" and that customer names and emails may have been taken. The bank says the two are not connected. Here is what Chase admitted, what doesn't add up, and what I actually think.

As reported to 19 November 2026 (morning, US Eastern):
• JPMorgan Chase statement (19 Nov): "third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack." The bank believes attackers accessed "certain marketing data held by those vendors", which may include some customer names and email addresses. It says there is no disruption to its services and "no connection" to the service disruption earlier in the week.
• Monday 16 Nov outage: Chase said it was a software bug in an on-premise hardware system, not cyber-related.
• The leak: Cybernews researchers report a released dataset with about 16,000 customer email addresses that appears to relate to Chase's Reserve card programme. Chase has not confirmed this.
• The timing: according to timelines reconstructed by Ostorlab and GoLocalProv from ransomware.live and Downdetector, the n0n extortion group listed Chase on its leak site at about 7:09 am Eastern on 16 Nov, and outage reports began at about 9:53 am. No one has shown the listing and the outage are connected.
• The same group claimed Expedia last week and has also listed Visa and Mastercard. Visa says the incident was at a third-party provider in Asia-Pacific, that its own systems were not involved, and that there is no indication card numbers were affected. Mastercard had made no statement as of these reports.

My take (opinion): a bug and a hack in the same week at the same bank is possible, and nobody has shown the outage was the hack. But "no connection" is a big claim three days in. "Okay, a little cyber" is my paraphrase, not a quote.

What to do: if your name and email were exposed, expect convincing fake Chase emails. Don't click links; open the app yourself or call the number on the back of your card.

General information as reported so far, plus clearly labelled opinion; not financial advice. A leak-site listing is a claim by criminals, not proof of a breach. The gang figure, the card and the scam email are illustrations. Logos are shown only to identify the organisations discussed. Meme images and sounds are brief reaction jokes, not statements by anyone shown. Not affiliated with or endorsed by any company named.

snippet.title: 앤트로픽 상장 대박인데 반도체는 폭락, 엔비디아 하이닉스 같이 무너진 진짜 이유
snippet.description:
+4.7%에서 -2.4%. 필라델피아 반도체 지수가 하루 안에 7%포인트를 뒤집었다. 앤트로픽이 상장한 바로 그날이다.

앤트로픽은 공모 조달금액 기준 역대 최대 IPO였고, 기관투자자 절반 이상이 공모주를 받지 못했다. 종가 기준으로는 17%대 급등 마감. 하지만 시가가 고가였고, 쭉 밀리면서 음봉으로 끝났다.

박시동 평론가는 못 받은 기관들이 앤트로픽을 사려고 다른 종목을 팔았고, 상장이라는 큰 이벤트가 끝나는 날에 다음 날이 옵션 만기라는 점을 짚었다. "이벤트가 끝나면 이제 잔치는 끝나는 거"라는 것. 이광수 소장은 "잔치를 해서 분위기가 좋았어야죠"라며, 잔치는 열리지도 않았다고 받아쳤다.

숫자는 이렇다. 엔비디아 -3.3%, 메타 -3.7%, 알파벳 -3.46%, 아마존 -3.87%, 하이닉스 -2.67%. 나스닥도 고점 대비 5% 가까이 밀렸다. 박시동 평론가는 "숏 자금이 이날 다 던진 것 같아요"라고 했고, 고점 대비로 보면 지지난주 검은 목요일(-5.5%)만큼의 충격이라고 봤다.

권다영 앵커가 전한 뱅크오브아메리카 펀드매니저 설문도 같은 쪽을 가리킨다. 바닥이 잡혔다고 보는 사람이 많지 않았고, 몇 달 안에 AI 투자가 줄어들 것 같다는 답이 많았다.

· 왜 다 같이 빠졌나 (18초)
· 앤트로픽 트레이드 (1분 58초)
· 다음 날 옵션 만기 (3분 20초)
